## Why "Wells-Du Bois"

`duboisR` is named for two data journalists who used quantitative methods
against the institutions that produced their data, rather than treating
those numbers as neutral:

- **W.E.B. Du Bois** pioneered statistical data visualization (most famously
  the 1900 Paris Exposition infographics) to document Black American life
  in a form white American statisticians of the era could not simply wave
  away. He also gave us *double consciousness* — the experience of seeing
  oneself simultaneously through one's own eyes and through the eyes of a
  society that measures and administers you.
- **Ida B. Wells** compiled and published statistical documentation of
  lynching (*The Red Record*, 1895) specifically to refute the era's
  official narrative that lynching was a response to crime — using the
  perpetrators' own reporting against them.

The protocol this package implements takes their shared method as a
starting point: administrative data produced by an institution is not a
transparent window onto the world that institution polices. It is a record
of *that institution's decisions*, shaped by whatever discretion, priorities,
and blind spots the institution itself has.

## Three theoretical pillars

**Critical Quantitative Foundations (QuantCrit).** Numbers are socially
constructed, not neutral. A `search_conducted` column is not a fact about
the world in the way a sensor reading is — it is a record of one officer's
discretionary decision, made under whatever incentives, training, and bias
that officer carried into the stop. Standard quantitative methods, applied
without this framing, can encode and launder that discretion as if it were
signal. `check_tendentious()` operationalizes this: it asks the researcher
to explicitly classify whether an outcome variable is an objective
measurement or an administrative/subjective decision, because the two
require different epistemic caution.

**Du Boisian double consciousness and institutional veils.** Administrative
police data measures *enforcement discretion*, not the underlying behavior
it is often assumed to proxy for. The `search_conducted` variable answers
"who did an officer choose to search," not "who was carrying contraband" —
the gap between those two questions is exactly the "veil" this package's
tools are built to help see past. The [Veil of Darkness
test](../reference/veil_of_darkness_test.html) is a direct, literal
instantiation of this idea: it uses a natural experiment (an officer's
reduced ability to observe race in the dark) to estimate how much of a
daytime racial disparity in stops survives when the "veil" of darkness
removes the officer's ability to act on race at all.

**Subpopulation and intersectional representation.** Aggregate statistics
can hide double standards of justice inside a single "average" number that
looks reassuring. `audit_composition()` and `subpopulation_disparities()`
exist to make that impossible by construction — they disaggregate by
subpopulation (including intersectionally, e.g. race × sex) rather than
reporting a single pooled figure, and `subpopulation_disparities()` reports
the FPR/FNR/PPV trade-off across subgroups explicitly rather than pretending
a single classifier can be simultaneously fair by every definition at once
(a mathematical impossibility once base rates differ — see Chouldechova
2017; Kleinberg, Mullainathan & Raghavan 2016).

## From theory to diagnostics: what each function checks for

| Protocol concern | Function |
|---|---|
| Is the outcome variable itself a proxy for human discretion, not an objective fact? | `check_tendentious()` |
| Does excluding a protected attribute actually remove its information, or is it encoded in "neutral" covariates? | `check_proxies()` |
| Are subpopulations represented, and is missingness itself patterned by subpopulation? | `audit_composition()` |
| Does a daytime racial disparity survive when officers can't see race? | `veil_of_darkness_test()` |
| Do apparent search/hit-rate disparities reflect different decision *thresholds*, or just different underlying risk distributions (infra-marginality)? | `aggregate_sufficient_statistics()` + `fit_threshold_test()` |
| Is a single model's error rate hiding starkly different error rates by subgroup? | `subpopulation_disparities()` |
| Has the researcher documented all of the above for anyone downstream who uses this dataset? | `use_datasheet()`, `build_datasheet_wizard()` |

None of these functions produce a verdict on whether a dataset or model "is
biased." They produce numbers a researcher needs to make that judgment
themselves, and — per the Datasheets for Datasets philosophy this package
also implements — they deliberately do not automate the qualitative
reflection that judgment requires.

- Gebru, T. et al. (2021). "Datasheets for Datasets." *Communications of
  the ACM*, 64(12), 86-92.
- Grogger, J. & Ridgeway, G. (2006). "Testing for Racial Profiling in
  Traffic Stops From Behind a Veil of Darkness." *Journal of the American
  Statistical Association*, 101(475), 878-887.
- Simoiu, C., Corbett-Davies, S., & Goel, S. (2017). "The problem of
  infra-marginality in outcome tests for discrimination." *Annals of
  Applied Statistics*, 11(3), 1193-1216.
- Pierson, E., Simoiu, C., Overgoor, J., Corbett-Davies, S., Ramachandran,
  V., Phillips, C., & Goel, S. (2020). "A large-scale analysis of racial
  disparities in police stops across the United States." *Nature Human
  Behaviour*, 4, 736-745.
- Chouldechova, A. (2017). "Fair prediction with disparate impact: A study
  of bias in recidivism prediction instruments." *Big Data*, 5(2), 153-163.
- Kleinberg, J., Mullainathan, S., & Raghavan, M. (2016). "Inherent
  Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores." *arXiv:1609.05807*.
- Benjamin, R. (2019). *Race After Technology: Abolitionist Tools for the
  New Jim Code*. Polity.
